title: 3-Read Friday #18: Skills vs Knowledge, Live Coaching, and Conceptual Understanding
author: Craig Barton
summary: Craig Barton's 3-Read Friday #18 curates three posts on curriculum philosophy and classroom coaching. Daisy Christodoulou revisits Scotland's Curriculum for Excellence thirteen years after it deliberately reduced content knowledge in favour of content-free skills statements, using a critical Sunday Times report -- and an admission from one of the curriculum's own architects -- to argue that skills cannot be taught directly without the knowledge that underpins them. Thahmina Begum examines what makes a teacher "coachable" during live, in-the-moment coaching, arguing that the success of the technique depends as much on how it is received as on how it is delivered. Dylan Kane sets out a practical framework for what conceptual understanding is actually good for -- course correction, flexibility, explaining why, choosing a strategy, and connecting to prior knowledge -- rather than treating it as a vague aspiration. Barton connects the three as different angles on getting more precise about what we mean by teaching well: knowing what knowledge underlies a skill, how coaching actually lands, and what conceptual understanding is for.
points: Daisy Christodoulou uses Keir Bloomer's own admission -- "we did not make sufficiently clear that skills are the accumulation of knowledge" -- to argue Scotland's skills-based curriculum has struggled for exactly the reason its critics predicted.

Thahmina Begum's "coachee continuum" reframes live coaching as a two-way responsibility: the coach's delivery matters, but so does whether the coachee treats it as a public opportunity rather than a threat to save face.

Dylan Kane's five uses of conceptual understanding -- course correction, flexibility, explaining why, choosing a strategy, connecting to prior knowledge -- give teachers concrete criteria for deciding whether an activity is worth doing.
Barton's throughline: all three posts push back against vague slogans (skills vs. knowledge, "be more coachable," "build conceptual understanding") in favour of precise, actionable definitions.
quotes: It’s the post that everyone has been reading this week, but I wanted to flag it up just in case you have missed it.
Daisy revisits the skills versus knowledge debate with the clarity and nuance that only she can, reflecting on the troubles that Scotland’s skill-based Curriculum for Excellence has encountered.
It was Thahmina who first introduced me to the concept of live coaching.
In this fantastic post, Thahmina digs deeper into the concept of live coaching, addressing one of the potential barriers: the ego of the person being coached!

Dylan does a far better job than I ever could of providing a framework to help us think about the role conceptual understanding plays in learning, and some concrete strategies to help our students acquire it.
